receta: situación del que mira + mecanismo en mapa real (Great Lakes)
destinatario: se lo manda alguien de Buffalo/Michigan a su amigo de otro estado que cree que nieva igual en todos lados, para explicarle por qué acá sí

interaccion.comentar: So which are you today: snow or sun? (one word, everyone can answer from where they live)

fuentes: National Weather Service, Winter Lake Effect Snow (weather.gov/safety/winter-lake-effect-snow): cold air, often from Canada, moves across the open waters of the Great Lakes; lake adds heat and moisture to the lowest layer of air; air rises, clouds merge into a narrow band producing 2 to 3 inches of snow per hour or more; snow can fall in one spot while sunshine is only a mile or two away
NWS Gaylord, Lake Effect Snow (weather.gov/apx/les): cold air over open Great Lakes water; lake-to-air temperature difference, fetch, elevation, shoreline orientation

frases.texto: Your town can be buried in snow while the next one over is sunny.
Cold air, often from Canada, blows across the Great Lakes.
The open water is relatively warm, so it adds heat and moisture to the air.
That air rises, and the clouds merge into a narrow band.
The National Weather Service says one band can drop two to three inches of snow an hour, or more.
Heads up: it's so narrow that the sun can be shining a mile or two away.
So which are you today: snow or sun?
Send this to the friend who swears it's snowing everywhere.
